identity.title: VersaPRM: Multi-Domain Process Reward Model via Synthetic Reasoning Data

problem.claim: Process reward models improve mathematical reasoning, but their use across non-mathematical domains is the task examined here.

gap.claim: Existing PRMs are predominantly trained on mathematical data, and their generalizability to non-mathematical domains has not been rigorously studied.

contributions.claim: Reports poor performance of current PRMs in domains beyond mathematics.
Introduces VersaPRM, a multi-domain PRM trained on synthetic reasoning data produced by a new data-generation and annotation method.
Open-sources the VersaPRM data, code, and models.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors distinguish VersaPRM through its multi-domain training and novel synthetic reasoning-data generation and annotation method.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report consistent performance gains across diverse domains for VersaPRM.
On MMLU-Pro Law, the authors report that VersaPRM with weighted majority voting gains 7.9% over the majority-voting baseline, compared with a 1.3% gain for Qwen2.5-Math-PRM.
The authors report that current PRMs perform poorly in other domains.

narrative_sequence.summary: PRMs are presented as useful for mathematical reasoning through increased inference-time computation.
The abstract notes mathematical-data concentration and limited rigorous study of non-mathematical generalizability.
The authors report poor performance of current PRMs outside mathematics.
VersaPRM is introduced using synthetic reasoning data generated and annotated by a new method.
The authors report cross-domain gains, give a Law-category comparison, and release the data, code, and models.

source_observation.claim: The abstract links a stated generalization gap to a domain-targeted model and supports the claim with one domain-specific percentage comparison.

lessons.interpretation: A focused problem–intervention–illustration chain can make a cross-domain contribution legible without listing every evaluation detail.
lessons.application: Frame a multi-domain method by naming the existing training concentration, the mechanism intended to address it, and one representative domain-specific comparison with baseline and competitor values.
lessons.exception: Avoid this compressed framing when domain coverage, evaluation conditions, or comparison definitions are essential to interpreting the claim but unavailable.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the diverse domains, evaluation protocol, dataset scale, or statistical uncertainty behind the reported gains.
The exact data-generation and annotation procedure and the scope of the claimed multi-domain performance are not described.
